tagline: A short mountain crossing climbs above Whitesburg toward Oven Fork.
intro: Pine Mountain Road carries US 119 over the ridge between Whitesburg and Oven Fork, crossing the Little Shepherd Trail along the way. Kentucky designated this 8.153-mile road as a scenic byway in 1995. The National Scenic Byway Foundation promotes the mountain views along the crossing. The ridge itself runs about 125 miles through Kentucky, Virginia and Tennessee, forming a long barrier to transportation. Only two waterways pass through the entire ridge: the Cumberland River at Pineville and the Clear Fork near Jellico, Tennessee.

The highway’s number changed as the national road network expanded. The Pineville-to-Jenkins section became US 123 in 1930, then US 119 in 1934 when that route reached Kentucky. Kentucky’s US 119 originally connected Pineville, Cumberland and Whitesburg by a series of two-lane roads paralleling the mountain. Later work widened parts of the mountain crossing to make it safer for trucks.

Start at US 119 and KY 15 in Whitesburg, in the valley of the North Fork of the Kentucky River. US 119 heads southwest over Pine Mountain, leaving the valley for the crossing. After the Little Shepherd Trail, the byway continues to the US 119 junction with KY 806 near Oven Fork.

moments.title: Whitesburg
moments.text: Whitesburg occupies the valley of the North Fork of the Kentucky River, below the US 119 crossing of Pine Mountain. The town began in 1842 on land Stephen Hiram Hogg offered for a county seat. First called Summit City, it was renamed for John D. White, who introduced the bill creating Letcher County. It remains the county seat. Here KY 15 meets US 119, which leads northeast toward Jenkins and southwest over the mountain toward Cumberland. The mountain crossing begins at that eastern end of KY 15; in the opposite direction, KY 15 connects Whitesburg with Hazard.

moments.title: Oven Fork
moments.text: Oven Fork lies on US 119 south of Whitesburg. Its name may have come from an oven used to fire bricks for local chimneys, or from German residents baking bread outdoors. The community’s first post office opened in 1879; a second opened in 1945 and closed in January 1993. The scenic byway ends near the community at the junction of US 119 and KY 806.

moments.title: Bad Branch Falls State Nature Preserve
moments.text: Bad Branch Falls drops 60 feet over sandstone cliffs in a narrow gorge cut into Pine Mountain. Trails and footbridges pass through a forest of hemlocks and mixed hardwoods. Tulip poplar, sweet birch, yellow birch and American beech grow with the hemlocks; flowering dogwood and rosebay rhododendron grow beneath the canopy. The gorge’s shaded, moist conditions support rare species including painted trillium and Fraser’s sedge. The original protected area, including the waterfall, was dedicated as a nature preserve in September 1985. Sandstone boulders and cliffs accompany the gorge’s streams, with ridgelines and knobs providing views into the Appalachians.
moments.notice: The waterfall drops over sandstone cliffs.
